analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to pay Medicare rebates on prescriptions filled for low-income seniors and disabled beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 17 senators, never left the Senate Finance Committee: after referral on April 23, 2015, the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare's prescription drug benefit, the government pays the full drug cost for its poorest enrollees — mostly low-income seniors and people with disabilities who also qualify for Medicaid — while drug manufacturers only have to give Medicaid-level discounts for drugs dispensed through Medicaid, not Medicare. This bill would have closed that gap: drug makers would have had to pay Medicare a rebate, set off the Medicaid rebate formula, for every covered prescription dispensed to those low-income enrollees. A manufacturer that refused to sign the rebate agreement would have had its drugs removed from Medicare Part D coverage. The rebates would be deposited into Medicare's prescription drug account, offsetting federal spending, and the bill explicitly excluded these new rebates from the Medicaid 'best price' calculation so manufacturers would not face double discounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicare beneficiaries — dual eligibles who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid — would benefit indirectly: the rebates would reduce federal Medicare drug spending, which in turn helps hold down premiums and taxpayer costs for everyone in the program. Taxpayers generally would gain from the estimated federal savings, and the government would gain leverage to keep drug prices down for the highest-cost, sickest beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Drug manufacturers would have to pay the Secretary of Health and Human Services a rebate for each Part D prescription dispensed to a 'rebate eligible' (low-income) individual, with the rebate amount tied to the Medicaid rebate formula.

A manufacturer that declined to sign the rebate agreement would have its drugs excluded from the definition of a covered Part D drug, meaning its products could not be billed to Medicare's drug benefit.
All rebate payments would be deposited into Medicare's Prescription Drug Account, offsetting federal Medicare drug spending.
The bill excluded the new Medicare rebates from the Medicaid 'best price' and average manufacturer price calculations, so manufacturers would not face stacking discounts across the two programs.

Prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans would be required to report dispensing and discount data so the government could compute the rebates, with civil money penalties of $10,000 per day for late reporting and up to $100,000 per false item.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost: they would pay a rebate on every prescription dispensed to low-income Part D enrollees, mirroring the discounts they already owe under Medicaid. The savings would come out of manufacturers' Part D revenues, which the Congressional Budget Office has historically found to be in the billions when similar proposals were scored.

drawbacks.text: Plans and insurers would bear new administrative burdens: prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage drug plans would have to report unit-level dispensing and discount data by National Drug Code for every rebate period, and would face civil money penalties of $10,000 per day for late reports and up to $100,000 per false item.

The enforcement mechanism cuts both ways for patients: if a manufacturer refused to sign the rebate agreement, its drugs would be excluded from Part D coverage, which could leave low-income patients without insurance coverage for those specific medicines.

The benefit to beneficiaries is indirect: the rebates flow into the Medicare program rather than to patients directly, so the gain arrives through lower premiums and federal savings rather than lower out-of-pocket drug costs at the pharmacy counter.

Drug manufacturers argued in public that extending Medicaid-style rebates to Medicare Part D amounted to price controls that would reduce revenues available for developing new medicines — the standard industry objection to every rebate-expansion proposal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a well-known pricing gap: the government pays full price through Medicare for drugs dispensed to its poorest enrollees while collecting Medicaid-level discounts only through Medicaid. The main costs fall on brand-name drug makers and on plan sponsors doing extra paperwork, and the main risk to patients — losing coverage for a non-participating manufacturer's drugs — is real but narrow. On balance the bill would have shifted billions in drug costs from taxpayers and Medicare premiums onto manufacturers, with the sharpest effect on the industry rather than on beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died at the end of the 114th Congress without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Nelson introduced the Medicare Drug Savings Act on April 23, 2015, with 16 original cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action appears in its history.
The bill required manufacturers to pay rebates on Part D drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees and excluded non-participating manufacturers' drugs from Medicare coverage.
The Finance Committee's record for this bill contains no hearings, no markups, and no votes during the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the bill never advanced, so they avoided paying the new rebates on low-income Medicare prescriptions and kept the existing Part D pricing arrangement intact. Low-income Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral to the Finance Committee; the action history shows no committee action of any kind.

against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Medicaid-style rebates to Medicare Part D, arguing it would function as government price controls on their products.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent — 15 Democrats and 2 Independents, with no Republicans — and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: They would have paid a Medicaid-formula rebate on every prescription dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, and a refusal would have cost them Medicare Part D coverage for their products. The bill's failure left their Part D revenues untouched.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans
industries.note: They would have taken on new reporting duties — dispensing and discount data by drug code, with fines up to $10,000 per day for late filings — but the rebates themselves would be paid by manufacturers, not plans, and the savings would help stabilize the program they operate in.
The bill excluded the new Medicare rebates from Medicaid's best price and average manufacturer price calculations, keeping Medicaid's own rebate system from being eroded by the new arrangement.
